Borrowed from Swedish å (“the letter å”). The letter was introduced into official Norwegian orthography in 1917, replacing the traditional Danish–Norwegian digraph ⟨aa⟩.
The character originated as an early modern German typographical innovation and entered Swedish through the printing press, appearing in works including Olaus Petri's catechism and the Swedish New Testament of 1526. Graphically, it developed from ⟨aa⟩, with the second ⟨a⟩ written above the first and gradually reduced to a ring.

1000080.etyen:
Borrowed from English Nigeria. The English name was formed from Niger (“Niger River”) and the placename-forming suffix -ia. Shaw proposed the name for the territories under British influence around the Niger River; it was subsequently applied to the British colony and, after independence in 1960, to the modern country.
The river name Niger is of uncertain origin. Store norske leksikon derives it from Tuareg Tuareg n'igherren (“flowing water; river”). Other etymologies have also been proposed, and the modern European spelling was probably influenced by Latin niger (“black”) rather than being de

1001872.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂m̥bʰi
Compound of the neuter form brått of brå (“hasty, sudden”) and om (“about, around”), literally approximately “hasty about”.
The first element brå is inherited from Old Norse bráðr (“hasty, sudden”), from Proto-Germanic *brēþaz (“rushed, in a hurry; quick”), ultimately related to the Proto-Indo-European root *bʰer- (“to boil, seethe”). The final element om continues Old Norse um (“around, about”), from Proto-Germanic *umbi (“around, about”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi (“around, about”).
Compare the parallel formation Swedish bråttom (“in a hurry, urgent”). T

1004688.etyen:
From fjell (“mountain”) + nabb (“peg, projection; rocky outcrop”). The first element is from Old Norse fjall (“mountain”), and the second element is from Old Norse nabbr (“peg, projection”), related to nebb (“beak, bill”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk fjellnabb (“small, sharp mountain projection”). Further compare Scots nabb and knab (“hillock, knoll; rocky protuberance”).
